questions.q: Define literal comprehension in your own words and give one example of a literal question from "Why the Novel Matters."
questions.a: Literal comprehension is the ability to identify information directly stated in the text without interpretation. Example: "What does Lawrence say is the 'simple truth' that eludes the philosopher or scientist?" (Answer: That nothing is important but life, and life exists only in the living.) A wrong answer would confuse literal with inferential, e.g., "Why does Lawrence think philosophers deny the body?" — that requires inference.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a literal and an inferential question using this excerpt: "The novel is the book of life. In this sense, the Bible is a great novel. You may say, it is about God. But it is really about man alive."
questions.a: Literal question: "What does Lawrence call the novel in this excerpt?" (Answer: "the book of life"). Inferential question: "Why does Lawrence describe the Bible as a 'great novel' despite its religious subject?" (Answer: Because it deals with 'man alive' — the living human experience — not abstract divinity). A wrong answer would treat both as literal or claim the inferential answer is "just an opinion" without textual anchoring.

questions.q: Read the lines: "If you're a parson, you talk about souls in heaven. If you're a novelist, you know that paradise is in the palm of your hand..." Answer: (a) Literal: What does the parson talk about? (b) Inferential: What does Lawrence imply about the novelist's view of paradise compared to the parson's?
questions.a: (a) Literal: The parson talks about souls in heaven. (b) Inferential: Lawrence implies the novelist values *embodied, tangible aliveness* (palm of hand, end of nose) over the parson's *abstract, afterlife paradise*. The novelist's paradise is immediate, sensory, and verifiable; the parson's is deferred and spiritual. A wrong answer would say "Lawrence hates religion" — an overgeneralization not supported by this excerpt alone.

questions.q:
Two students answer: "Why does Lawrence compare the philosopher to a rabbit making pills?" 
Student A: "Because philosophers think thinking is the only thing that matters, just like a rabbit thinks its pills are the only thing that matters." 
Student B: "Lawrence uses absurdity to show that privileging one human faculty (thought) over the whole living organism is as ridiculous as a rabbit valuing only its pellets." 
Analyze which answer demonstrates stronger inferential comprehension and why.
questions.a: Student B is stronger. Student A merely paraphrases the simile (literal-level understanding of the comparison). Student B *infers the rhetorical purpose*: Lawrence uses reductio ad absurdum to critique the philosopher's fragmentation of human experience. Student B connects the analogy to the essay's central argument (wholeness vs. parts) — a hallmark of deep inferential comprehension. A wrong evaluation would call them "equally good" because both mention the rabbit.

questions.q: Evaluate this inference: "Lawrence believes science is useless because it only studies dead bodies." Is this a valid inference from the text? Justify with evidence.
questions.a: Invalid inference — it overstates Lawrence's position. The text says: "To the scientist, I am dead. He puts under the microscope a bit of dead me, and calls it me." Lawrence critiques the *reductionist method* (studying parts in isolation), not science's utility. He acknowledges scientific knowledge ("my heart, my liver... have all been scientifically me") but denies it captures the *whole living man*. A valid inference: "Lawrence argues science cannot grasp the living whole because its method requires dissection." A wrong evaluation would accept the student's claim as "basically true" without noticing the exaggeration.

questions.q: From the paragraph beginning "Me, man alive, I am a very curious assembly of incongruous parts..." create ONE literal question and ONE inferential question that a Class 12 exam might ask.
questions.a: Literal: "According to Lawrence, what happens if a person tries to define their integrity by saying 'I am this, I am that'?" (Answer: They turn into a 'stupid fixed thing like a lamp-post.') Inferential: "Why does Lawrence use the metaphor of 'ideal corsets' to describe self-definition?" (Answer: To show that even 'ideal' self-concepts are rigid, external constraints that cannot accommodate the fluid, changing nature of aliveness — just as corsets restrict the body despite being fashionable.) A poor answer would create two literal questions or an inferential question answerable by direct quote.
